pharm: Allylamine antifungal; inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis
quick: Limited human data; animal studies show no harm
Avoid if CrCl <50 mL/min (use not recommended)
summary: Oral terbinafine is an allylamine antifungal indicated for onychomycosis of the toenail or fingernail due to dermatophytes (tinea unguium), confirmed by KOH, culture, or biopsy. It is fungicidal via squalene epoxidase inhibition. Key safety concerns include rare but serious hepatotoxicity (including liver failure), persistent taste/smell disturbance, severe skin reactions, neutropenia, and depressive symptoms.
indications: Onychomycosis of the toenail or fingernail due to dermatophytes (tinea unguium), with diagnosis confirmed by KOH preparation, fungal culture, or nail biopsy

dosage.n: Optimal clinical effect seen months after mycological cure, as healthy nail regrows.
Evaluate for chronic/active liver disease before initiating. Optimal effect seen months after treatment ends.

admin: Obtain nail specimen (KOH, culture, or biopsy) to confirm dermatophyte onychomycosis before treating
Evaluate for evidence of chronic or active liver disease before initiating
May be taken with or without food
Reassess liver function periodically during therapy
Discontinue if liver injury, taste/smell disturbance, severe skin reaction, or neutropenia develops
moa: Allylamine antifungal that inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, an enzyme in the ergosterol biosynthesis pathway (independent of cytochrome P450). This blocks conversion of squalene to lanosterol, causing ergosterol deficiency and toxic intracellular squalene accumulation, which is fungicidal against dermatophytes.

absolute: History of allergic reaction to oral terbinafine (risk of anaphylaxis)
relative: Renal impairment (CrCl <=50 mL/min) - use not recommended
monitor: Complete blood count if signs of infection or prolonged therapy

preg: Available postmarketing human data are insufficient to assess drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. Animal reproduction studies (rats and rabbits) showed no malformations or fetal harm at up to 23x and 12x the maximum recommended human dose. Treatment of onychomycosis can generally be postponed until after pregnancy.
lact: Terbinafine is present in human milk after oral administration. There are no data on effects on the breastfed infant or on milk production; because of limited benefit of treating a non-urgent condition, breastfeeding is generally not recommended during therapy.
renal: In patients with renal impairment (CrCl <=50 mL/min), terbinafine clearance is reduced by approximately 50%. Use of oral terbinafine in this population has not been adequately studied and is not recommended.
hepatic: Contraindicated in patients with chronic or active liver disease. Liver failure, sometimes leading to liver transplant or death, has occurred, including in patients with no preexisting liver disease. Obtain baseline transaminases, monitor periodically, and discontinue if liver injury develops. Clearance is reduced ~50% in hepatic cirrhosis.

major: CYP2D6 substrates (tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, beta-blockers, class 1C antiarrhythmics such as flecainide/propafenone, MAO-B inhibitors) - terbinafine is a CYP2D6 inhibitor; monitor and consider dose reduction. Effect on desipramine persisted up to 4 weeks after stopping.
Rifampin - increases terbinafine clearance (~100%), reducing efficacy
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food increases the AUC by less than 20%.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol; potential additive hepatotoxicity given the risk of drug-induced liver injury.
interactions.diagnostics: Liver enzyme abnormalities are common; obtain pretreatment and periodic transaminases. Severe neutropenia (ANC <=1000 cells/mm3) warrants discontinuation.

serious: Severe taste loss or smell loss (may be prolonged or permanent)
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
emergency: Acute liver failure (jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain)

monitoring: Serum transaminases at baseline (pretreatment) and periodically during therapy
Complete blood count if prolonged therapy or signs of infection
counsel: Take once daily, with or without food, for the full prescribed course (6 weeks fingernail, 12 weeks toenail)
Nail appearance improves slowly over months as a healthy nail grows out, even after treatment ends
Report immediately signs of liver injury: persistent nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue, yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, or abdominal pain
Report any change or loss of taste or smell - stop the drug and contact your doctor
Report rash, blistering, or skin peeling, and any mood changes/depression
pk: Peak plasma ~1 mcg/mL at 2 h after 250 mg dose
Persists in skin/nail/sebum for weeks after stopping
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light
pearls: Allylamine acts on squalene epoxidase (not CYP-dependent like azoles); fungicidal against dermatophytes
Confirm dermatophyte onychomycosis by KOH/culture/biopsy before committing to long treatment
Bioavailability ~40% due to first-pass metabolism; food effect is negligible
Potent CYP2D6 inhibitor - watch TCAs, SSRIs, beta-blockers, and class 1C antiarrhythmics; effect can persist weeks after stopping
Taste and smell disturbances can be severe and occasionally permanent
Avoid in renal impairment (CrCl <=50 mL/min) - clearance halved and use not studied
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue the regular once-daily schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Clinical overdose experience is limited; doses up to 5 grams (20x the daily dose) have been taken without serious adverse reactions. Symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, rash, frequent urination, and headache. Treatment is supportive (consider activated charcoal and symptomatic care).
